entries.09bea8638514c4cc4791e8e2944b719085962986: <div sID="gen9088" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="8" osisID="Esth.8" sID="Esth.8"/> <div eID="gen9088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9089" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen9090" type="x-p"/> We left the plotter hanging, and are now to see what becomes of his plot. I. His plot was to raise an estate for himself; and all his estate, being confiscated for treason, is given to Esther and Mordecai, <reference osisRef="Esth.8.1-Esth.8.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. His plot was to ruin the Jews; and as to that, 1. Esther earnestly intercedes for the reversing of the edict against them, <reference osisRef="Esth.8.3-Esth.8.6">ver. 3-6</reference>. 2. It is in effect done by another edict, here published, empowering the Jews to stand up in their own defence against their enemies, <reference osisRef="Esth.8.7-Esth.8.14">ver. 7-14</reference>. III. This occasions great joy to the Jews and all their friends, <reference osisRef="Esth.8.15-Esth.8.17">ver. 15-17</reference>.
entries.d21cd8ad4fc7e3d0dfe31e03e38a30cdc12a7b48: <div eID="gen9090" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen9089" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Esther and Mordecai Enriched. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 510.)</title> <div sID="gen9091" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> On that day did the king Ahasuerus give the house of Haman the Jews' enemy unto Esther the queen. And Mordecai came before the king; for Esther had told what he <hi type="italic">was</hi> unto her. <hi type="super">2</hi> And the king took off his ring, which he had taken from Haman, and gave it unto Mordecai. And Esther set Mordecai over the house of Haman. <div eID="gen9091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9092" type="x-p"/> It was but lately that we had Esther and Mordecai in tears and in fears, but fasting and praying; now let us see how to them there arose light in darkness. Here is, 1. Esther enriched. Haman was hanged as a traitor, therefore his estate was forfeited to the crown, and the king gave it all to Esther, in recompence for the fright that wicked man had put her into and the vexation he had created her, <reference osisRef="Esth.8.1">v. 1</reference>. His houses and lands, good sand chattels, and all the money he had heaped up which he was prime-minister of state (which, we may suppose, was no little), are given to Esther; they are all her own, added to the allowance she already had. Thus is <hi type="italic">the wealth of the sinner laid up for the just,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">innocent divides the silver,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.13.22">Prov. xiii. 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.27.17-Job.27.18">Job xxvii. 17, 18</reference>. What Haman would have done mischief with Esther will do good with; and estates are to be valued as they are used. 2. Mordecai advanced. His pompous procession, this morning, through the streets of the city, was but a sudden flash or blaze of honour; but here we have the more durable and gainful preferments to which he was raised, which yet the other happily made way for. (1.) He is now owned as the queen's cousin, which till now, though Esther had been four years queen, for aught that appears, the king did not know. So humble, so modest, a man was Mordecai, and so far from being ambitious of a place at court, that he concealed his relation to the queen and her obligations to him as her guardian, and never made us of her interest for any advantage of his own. Who but Mordecai could have taken so little notice of so great an honour? But now he was brought <hi type="italic">before the king,</hi> introduced, as we say, to kiss his hand; for now, at length, <hi type="italic">Esther had told what he was to her,</hi> not only near a-kin to her, but the best friend she had in the world, who took care of her when she was an orphan, and one whom she still respected as a father. Now the king finds himself, for his wife's sake, more obliged than he thought he had been to delight in doing honour to Mordecai. How great were the merits of that man to whom both king and queen did in effect owe their lives! Being brought before the king, to him no doubt he bowed, and did reverence, though he would not to Haman an Amalekite. (2.) The king makes his lord privy-seal in the room of Haman. All the trust he had reposed in Haman, and all the power he had given him, are here transferred to Mordecai; for the ring which he had taken from Haman he gave to Mordecai, and made this trusty humble man as much his favourite, his confidant, and his agent, as ever that proud perfidious wretch was; a happy change he made of his bosom-friends, and so, no doubt, he and his people soon found it. (3.) The queen makes him here steward, for the management of Haman's estate, and for getting and keeping possession of it: <hi type="italic">She set Mordecai over the house of Haman.</hi> See the vanity of laying up treasure upon earth; he that <hi type="italic">heapeth up riches knoweth not who shall gather them</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.39.6">Ps. xxxix. 6</reference>), not only <hi type="italic">whether he shall be a wise man or a fool</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.19">Eccl. ii. 19</reference>), but whether he shall be a friend or an enemy. With what little pleasure, nay, with what constant vexation, would Haman have looked upon his estate if he could have foreseen that Mordecai, the man he hated above all men in the world, should have <hi type="italic">rule over all that wherein he had laboured,</hi> and thought that he showed himself wise! It is our interest, therefore, to make sure those riches which will not be left behind, but will go with us to another world.
entries.66487c1daf2f469756218d1c1e5e4090e0ddd1d8: <div eID="gen9092" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Jews Encouraged to Self-Defence. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 510.)</title> <div sID="gen9093" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> And Esther spake yet again before the king, and fell down at his feet, and besought him with tears to put away the mischief of Haman the Agagite, and his device that he had devised against the Jews. <hi type="super">4</hi> Then the king held out the golden sceptre toward Esther. So Esther arose, and stood before the king, <hi type="super">5</hi> And said, If it please the king, and if I have found favour in his sight, and the thing <hi type="italic">seem</hi> right before the king, and I <hi type="italic">be</hi> pleasing in his eyes, let it be written to reverse the letters devised by Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, which he wrote to destroy the Jews which <hi type="italic">are</hi> in all the king's provinces: <hi type="super">6</hi> For how can I endure to see the evil that shall come unto my people? or how can I endure to see the destruction of my kindred? <hi type="super">7</hi> Then the king Ahasuerus said unto Esther the queen and to Mordecai the Jew, Behold, I have given Esther the house of Haman, and him they have hanged upon the gallows, because he laid his hand upon the Jews. <hi type="super">8</hi> Write ye also for the Jews, as it liketh you, in the king's name, and seal <hi type="italic">it</hi> with the king's ring: for the writing which is written in the king's name, and sealed with the king's ring, may no man reverse. <hi type="super">9</hi> Then were the king's scribes called at that time in the third month, that <hi type="italic">is,</hi> the month Sivan, on the three and twentieth <hi type="italic">day</hi> thereof; and it was written according to all that Mordecai commanded unto the Jews, and to the lieutenants, and the deputies and rulers of the provinces which <hi type="italic">are</hi> from India unto Ethiopia, a hundred twenty and seven provinces, unto every province according to the writing thereof, and unto every people after their language, and to the Jews according to their writing, and according to their language. <hi type="super">10</hi> And he wrote in the king Ahasuerus' name, and sealed <hi type="italic">it</hi> with the king's ring, and sent letters by posts on horseback, <hi type="italic">and</hi> riders on mules, camels, <hi type="italic">and</hi> young dromedaries: <hi type="super">11</hi> Wherein the king granted the Jews which <hi type="italic">were</hi> in every city to gather themselves together, and to stand for their life, to destroy, to slay, and to cause to perish, all the power of the people and province that would assault them, <hi type="italic">both</hi> little ones and women, and <hi type="italic">to take</hi> the spoil of them for a prey, <hi type="super">12</hi> Upon one day in all the provinces of king Ahasuerus, <hi type="italic">namely,</hi> upon the thirteenth <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the twelfth month, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> the month Adar. <hi type="super">13</hi> The copy of the writing for a commandment to be given in every province <hi type="italic">was</hi> published unto all people, and that the Jews should be ready against that day to avenge themselves on their enemies. <hi type="super">14</hi> <hi type="italic">So</hi> the posts that rode upon mules <hi type="italic">and</hi> camels went out, being hastened and pressed on by the king's commandment. And the decree was given at Shushan the palace. <div eID="gen9093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9094" type="x-p"/> Haman, the chief enemy of the Jews, was hanged, Mordecai and Esther, their chief friends, were sufficiently protected; but many others there were in the king's dominions that hated the Jews and desired their ruin, and to their rage and malice all the rest of that people lay exposed; for the edict against them was still in force, and, in pursuance of it, their enemies would on the day appointed fall upon them, and they would be deemed as rebels against the king and his government if they should offer to resist and take up arms in their own defence. For the preventing of this, <div eID="gen9094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9095" type="x-p"/> I. The queen here makes intercession with much affection and importunity. She came, a second time, uncalled into the king's presence (<reference osisRef="Esth.8.3">v. 3</reference>), and was as before encouraged to present her petition, by the king's holding out the golden sceptre to her, <reference osisRef="Esth.8.4">v. 4</reference>. Her petition is that the king, having put away Haman, would put away the mischief of Haman and his device against the Jews, that that might not take place now that he was taken off. Many a man's mischief survives him, and the wickedness he devised operates when he is gone. What men project and write may, after their death, be either very profitable or very pernicious. It was therefore requisite in this case that, for the defeating of Haman's plot, they should apply to the king for a further act of grace, that by another edict he would reverse the letters devised by Haman, and which he wrote (she does not say which the king <hi type="italic">consented to and confirmed with his own seal;</hi> she leaves it to his own conscience to say that), by which he took an effectual course to <hi type="italic">destroy the Jews in all the king's provinces,</hi> <reference osisRef="Esth.8.5">v. 5</reference>. If the king were indeed, as he seemed to be, troubled that such a decree was made, he could not do less than revoke it; for what is repentance, but undoing, to the utmost of our power, what we have done amiss? 1. This petition Esther presents with much affection: She <hi type="italic">fell down at the king's feet and besought him with tears</hi> (<reference osisRef="Esth.8.3">v. 3</reference>), every tear as precious as any of the pearls with which she was adorned. It was time to be earnest when the church of God lay at stake. Let none be so great as to be unwilling to stoop, none so merry as to be unwilling to weep, when thereby they may do any service to God's church and people. Esther, though safe herself, fell down, and begged with tears for the deliverance of her people. 2. She expresses it with great submission, and a profound deference to the king and his wisdom and will (<reference osisRef="Esth.8.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">If it please the king and if I have found favour in his sight</hi>—and again, "If the thing itself seem right and reasonable before the king, and if I that ask it <hi type="italic">be pleasing in his eyes,</hi> let the decree be reversed." Even when we have the utmost reason and justice on our side, and have the clearest cause to plead, yet it becomes us to speak to our superiors with humility and modesty, and all possible expressions of respect, and not to talk like demandants when we are supplicants. There is nothing lost be decency and good breeding. As <hi type="italic">soft answers turn away wrath,</hi> so soft askings obtain favour. 3. She enforces her petition with a pathetic plea: "<hi type="italic">For how can I endure to see the evil that shall come upon my people?</hi> Little comfort can I have of my own life if I cannot prevail for theirs: as good share in the evil myself as see it come upon them; for <hi type="italic">how can I endure to see the destruction of my kindred,</hi> that are dear to me?" Esther, a queen, owns her poor kindred, and speaks of them with a very tender concern. Now it was that she mingled her tears with her words, that <hi type="italic">she wept and made supplication;</hi> we read of no tears when she begged for her own life, but, now that she was sure of that, she wept for her people. Tears of pity and tenderness are the most Christ-like. Those that are truly concerned for the public would rather die in the last ditch than live to see the desolations of the church of God and the ruin of their country. Tender spirits cannot bear to think of the destruction of their people and kindred, and therefore dare not omit any opportunity of giving them relief. <div eID="gen9095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9096" type="x-p"/> II. The king here takes a course for the preventing of the mischief that Haman had designed. 1. The king knew, and informed the queen, that, according to the constitution of the Persian government, the former edict could not be revoked (<reference osisRef="Esth.8.8">v. 8</reference>): What is <hi type="italic">written in the king's name, and sealed with the king's ring,</hi> may not, under any pretence whatsoever, be reversed. This was a fundamental article of their <hi type="italic">magna charta,</hi> that no law or decree, when once it had passed the royal assent, could be repealed or recalled, no judgment vacated, no attainder reversed, <reference osisRef="Dan.6.15">Dan. vi. 15</reference>. This is so far from bespeaking the wisdom and honour of the Medes and Persians that really it bespeaks their pride and folly, and consequently their shame. It is ridiculous in itself for any man, or company of men, to pretend to such an infallibility of wisdom as to foresee all the consequences of what they decree; and therefore it is unjust, and injurious to mankind, to claim such a supremacy of power as to make their decrees irrevocable, whether the consequences prove good or bad. This savours of that old presumption which ruined us all: <hi type="italic">We will be as gods.</hi> Much more prudent is that proviso of our constitution, that no law can, by any words or sanctions whatsoever, be made unrepealable, any more than any estate unalienable. <hi type="italic">Cujus est instruere, ejus est destruere—the right to enact implies the right to repeal.</hi> It is God's prerogative not to repent, and to say what can never be altered or unsaid. 2. Yet he found an expedient to undo the devices of Haman, and defeat his design, by signing and publishing another decree to authorize the Jews to stand upon their defence, <hi type="italic">vim vi repellere, et invasorem occidere—to oppose force to force, and destroy the assailant.</hi> This would be their effectual security. The king shows them that he had done enough already to convince them that he had a concern for the Jewish nation, for he had ordered his favourite to be hanged <hi type="italic">because he laid his hand upon the Jews</hi> (<reference osisRef="Esth.8.7">v. 7</reference>), and he therefore would do the utmost he could to protect them; and he leaves it as fully with Esther and Mordecai to use his name and power for their deliverance as before he had left it with Haman to use his name and power for their destruction: <hi type="italic">"Write for the Jews as it liketh you</hi> (<reference osisRef="Esth.8.8">v. 8</reference>), saving only the honour of our constitution. Let the mischief be put away as effectually as may be without reversing the letters." The secretaries of state were ordered to attend to draw up this edict on the twenty-third day of the third month (<reference osisRef="Esth.8.9">v. 9</reference>), about two months after the promulgation of the former, but nine months before the time set for its execution: it was to be drawn up and published in the respective languages of all the provinces. Shall the subjects of an earthly prince have his decrees in a language they understand? and shall God's oracles and laws be locked up from his servants in an unknown tongue? It was to be directed to the proper officers of every province, both to the justices of peace and to the deputy-lieutenants. It was to be carefully dispersed throughout all the king's dominions, and true copies sent by expresses to all the provinces. The purport of this decree was to commission the Jews, upon the day which was appointed for their destruction, to draw together in a body for their own defence. And, (1.) To stand for their life, that, whoever assaulted them, it might be at their peril. (2.) They might not only act defensively, but might <hi type="italic">destroy, and slay, and cause to perish, all the power of the people that would assault them, men, women, and children</hi> (<reference osisRef="Esth.8.11">v. 11</reference>), and thus <hi type="italic">to avenge themselves on their enemies</hi> (<reference osisRef="Esth.8.13">v. 13</reference>), and, if they pleased, to enrich themselves by their enemies, for they were empowered to take the spoil of them for a prey. Now, [1.] This showed his kindness to the Jews, and sufficiently provided for their safety; for he latter decree would be looked upon as a tacit revocation of the former, though not in expression. But, [2.] It shows the absurdity of that branch of their constitution that none of the king's edicts might be repealed; for it laid the king here under a necessity of enacting a civil war in his own dominions, between the Jews and their enemies, so that both sides took up arms <hi type="italic">by</hi> his authority, and yet <hi type="italic">against</hi> his authority. No better could come of men's pretending to be wise above what is given them. Great expedition was used in dispersing this decree, the king himself being in pain lest it should come too late and any mischief should be done to the Jews by virtue of the former decree before the notice of this arrived. It was therefore <hi type="italic">by the king's commandment,</hi> as well as Mordecai's, that the messengers were <hi type="italic">hastened and pressed on</hi> (<reference osisRef="Esth.8.14">v. 14</reference>), and had swift beasts provided them, <reference osisRef="Esth.8.10">v. 10</reference>. It was not a time to trifle when so many lives were in danger.
entries.67a0218ebafc1c9b822c6914d56463a1080788b7: <div eID="gen9096" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Joy of the Jews. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 510.)</title> <div sID="gen9097" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> And Mordecai went out from the presence of the king in royal apparel of blue and white, and with a great crown of gold, and with a garment of fine linen and purple: and the city of Shushan rejoiced and was glad. <hi type="super">16</hi> The Jews had light, and gladness, and joy, and honour. <hi type="super">17</hi> And in every province, and in every city, whithersoever the king's commandment and his decree came, the Jews had joy and gladness, a feast and a good day. And many of the people of the land became Jews; for the fear of the Jews fell upon them. <div eID="gen9097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9098" type="x-p"/> It was but a few days ago that we had Mordecai in sackcloth and all the Jews in sorrow; but here is a blessed change, Mordecai in purple and all the Jews in joy. See <reference osisRef="Ps.30.5">Ps. xxx. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.30.11">11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.30.12">12</reference>. 1. Mordecai in purple, <reference osisRef="Esth.8.15">v. 15</reference>. Having obtained an order for the relief of all the Jews, he was easy, he parted with his mourning weeds, and put on the <hi type="italic">royal apparel,</hi> which either belonged to his place or which the king appointed him as a favourite. His robes were rich, <hi type="italic">blue and white, of fine linen and purple;</hi> so was his coronet: it was <hi type="italic">of gold.</hi> These are things not worth taking notice of, but as they were marks of the king's favour, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> the fruit of God's favour to his church. It is well with a land when the ensigns of dignity are made the ornaments of serious piety. The <hi type="italic">city Shushan</hi> was sensible of its advantage in the preferment of Mordecai, and therefore <hi type="italic">rejoiced and was glad,</hi> not only pleased in general with the advancement of virtue, but promising itself, in particular, better times, now that so good a man was entrusted with power. Haman was hanged; <hi type="italic">and, when the wicked perish, there is shouting,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.11.10">Prov. xi. 10</reference>. Mordecai was preferred; and, <hi type="italic">when the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice.</hi> 2. The Jews in joy, <reference osisRef="Esth.8.16-Esth.8.17">v. 16, 17</reference>. The Jews, who awhile ago were under a dark cloud, dejected and disgraced, now had <hi type="italic">light and gladness, joy and honour, a feast and a good lay.</hi> If they had not been threatened and in distress they would not have had occasion for this extraordinary joy. Thus are God's people sometimes made <hi type="italic">to sow in tears</hi> that they may <hi type="italic">reap in</hi> so much the more <hi type="italic">joy.</hi> The suddenness and strangeness of the turn of affairs in their favour added much to their joy. They were <hi type="italic">like those that dream; then was their mouth filled with laughter,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.126.1-Ps.126.2">Ps. cxxvi. 1, 2</reference>. One good effect of this deliverance was that <hi type="italic">many of the people of the land,</hi> that were considerate, sober, and well inclined, became Jews, were proselyted to the Jewish religion, renounced idolatry, and worshipped the true God only. Haman thought to extirpate the Jews, but it proves, in the issue, that their numbers are greatly increased and many added to the church. Observe, When <hi type="italic">the Jews had joy and gladness</hi> then <hi type="italic">many of the people of the land became Jews.</hi> The holy cheerfulness of those that profess religion is a great ornament to their profession, and will invite and encourage others to be religious. The reason here given why so many became Jews at this time is because <hi type="italic">the fear of the Jews fell upon them.</hi> When they observed how wonderfully divine Providence had owned them and wrought for them in this critical juncture, (1.) They thought them great, and considered those happy that were among them; and therefore they came over to them, as was foretold, <reference osisRef="Zech.8.23">Zech. viii. 23</reference>. <hi type="italic">We will go with you, for we have heard,</hi> we have seen, <hi type="italic">that God is with you, the shield of your help, and the sword of your excellency,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.33.29">Deut. xxxiii. 29</reference>. When the church prospers, and is smiled upon, many will come into it that will be shy of it when it is in trouble. (2.) They thought them formidable, and considered those miserable that were against them. They plainly saw in Haman's fate that, if any offered injury to the Jews, it was at their peril; and therefore, for their own security, they joined themselves to them. It is folly to think of contending with the God of Israel, and therefore it is wisdom to think of submitting to him.  <chapter eID="Esth.8"/> <div eID="gen9098" type="x-p"/>

entries.ccc928841e58334081470883a21c6faa895b9085: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4441"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 8</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Esth.8.1-Esth.8.6">Es 8:1-6</reference>. Mordecai Advanced.</title> <div sID="gen6422" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4441"/><hi type="bold">1. On that day did the king Ahasuerus give the house of Haman ... unto Esther--</hi>His property was confiscated, and everything belonging to him, as some compensation for the peril to which she had been exposed.<div eID="gen6422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6423" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Mordecai came before the king--</hi>that is, was introduced at court and appointed one of the seven counsellors. Esther displayed great prudence and address in acknowledging Mordecai's relation to her at the moment most fitted to be of eminent service to him. <div eID="gen6423" type="x-p"/>
entries.2985d80d909df69e4c9ecca5c07eb06d70dac0bb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4442"/><div sID="gen6424" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4442"/><hi type="bold">2. the king took off his ring, ... and gave it unto Mordecai--</hi>By that act transferring to him all the power and authority which the ring symbolized, and promoting him to the high dignity which Haman had formerly filled.<div eID="gen6424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6425" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Esther set Mordecai over the house of Haman--</hi>as her steward or factor, to manage that large and opulent estate which had been assigned to her. <div eID="gen6425" type="x-p"/>
entries.e408f744728458ae799cfde66cad9d1dd633044f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4443"/><div sID="gen6426" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4443"/><hi type="bold">3. Esther spake yet again before the king, and fell down at his feet--</hi>The king was then not reclining at table, but sitting on a divan, most probably in the Persian attitude, leaning back against the cushions, and one foot under him.<div eID="gen6426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6427" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">besought him with tears to put away the mischief of Haman--</hi>that is, to repeal the sanguinary edict which, at the secret instigation of Haman, had been recently passed (<reference osisRef="Esth.3.12">Es 3:12</reference>). <div eID="gen6427" type="x-p"/>
entries.8e43e24054ddeef67444cadb10df5571eb041124: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4444"/><div sID="gen6428" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4444"/><hi type="bold">4. Then the king held out the golden sceptre toward Esther--</hi>in token that her request was accepted, and that she needed no longer to maintain the humble attitude of a suppliant. <div eID="gen6428" type="x-p"/>
entries.487c4020c4ce6cf63cc140143c0cbc296c561602: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4445"/><div sID="gen6429" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4445"/><hi type="bold">5-6. reverse the letters devised by Haman ... to destroy the Jews--</hi>The whole conduct of Esther in this matter is characterized by great tact, and the variety of expressions by which she describes her willing submission to her royal husband, the address with which she rolls the whole infamy of the meditated massacre on Haman, and the argument she draws from the king's sanction being surreptitiously obtained, that the decree should be immediately reversed--all indicate the queen's wisdom and skill, and she succeeded in this point also. <div eID="gen6429" type="x-p"/>
entries.dd8fe187f7b589b9e74ac1526847ef1bc854abe5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4446"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Esth.8.7-Esth.8.14">Es 8:7-14</reference>. Ahasuerus Grants to the Jews to Defend Themselves.</title> <div sID="gen6430" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4446"/><hi type="bold">8. Write ... in the king's name, and seal it with the king's ring--</hi>Hence it is evident that the royal ring had a seal in it, which, being affixed to any document, authenticated it with the stamp of royal authority.<div eID="gen6430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6431" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which ... may no man reverse--</hi>This is added as the reason why he could not comply with the queen's request for a direct reversal or recall of Haman's letters; namely, that the laws of the Medes and Persians, once passed, were irrevocable. <div eID="gen6431" type="x-p"/>
entries.262d49b9e17afe46e1d02269712a8f757433c207: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4447"/><div sID="gen6432" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4447"/><hi type="bold">10. sent ... by posts ... and riders on ... camels, and young dromedaries--</hi>The business being very urgent, the swiftest kind of camel would be employed, and so the word in the original denotes the wind-camel. Young dromedaries also are used to carry expresses, being remarkable for the nimbleness and ease of their movements. Animals of this description could convey the new rescript of Ahasuerus over the length and breadth of the Persian empire in time to relieve the unhappy Jews from the ban under which they lay. <div eID="gen6432" type="x-p"/>
entries.c03e091f289002665fba085cbc0c34315f61d4c1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4448"/><div sID="gen6433" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4448"/><hi type="bold">11-13. the king granted the Jews ... to stand for their life ... to slay ... all ... that would assault them--</hi>The fixed and unalterable character claimed for Persian edicts often placed the king in a very awkward dilemma; for, however bitterly he might regret things done in a moment of haste and thoughtlessness, it was beyond even his power to prevent the consequences. This was the reason on account of which the king was laid under a necessity not to reverse, but to issue a contradictory edict; according to which it was enacted that if, pursuant to the first decree, the Jews were assaulted, they might, by virtue of the second, defend themselves and even slay their enemies. However strange and even ridiculous this mode of procedure may appear, it was the only one which, from the peculiarities of court etiquette in Persia, could be adopted. Instances occur in sacred (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.14">Da 6:14</reference>), no less than profane, history. Many passages of the Bible attest the truth of this, particularly the well-known incident of Daniel's being cast into the den of lions, in conformity with the rash decree of Darius, though, as it afterwards appeared, contrary to the personal desire of that monarch. That the law of Persia has undergone no change in this respect, and the power of the monarch not less immutable, appear from many anecdotes related in the books of modern travellers through that country. <div eID="gen6433" type="x-p"/>
entries.3d9987fc923346b8f922e2f31438be88ed12c8fe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4449"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Esth.8.15-Esth.8.17">Es 8:15-17</reference>. Mordecai's Honors, and the Jews' Joy.</title> <div sID="gen6434" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4449"/><hi type="bold">15. Mordecai went out ... in royal apparel--</hi>He was invested with the khelaat of official honor. A dress of blue and white was held in great estimation among the Persians; so that Mordecai, whom the king delighted to honor, was in fact arrayed in the royal dress and insignia. The variety and the kind of insignia worn by a favorite at once makes known to the people the particular dignity to which he has been raised. <chapter eID="Esth.8"/>

entries.ae013d33d4a071174f9603bde31af0f6d9233b54: <div eID="gen15590" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen15591" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15592" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15592" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15591" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15593" type="x-p"/> Ahasuerus invests Mordecai with the offices and dignities possessed by Haman, <reference osisRef="Est.8.1">Est 8:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Est.8.2">Est 8:2</reference>. Esther begs that the decree of destruction gone out against the Jews may be reversed, <reference osisRef="Est.8.3-Est.8.6">Est 8:3-6</reference>. He informs her that the acts that had once passed the kings seal cannot be reversed; but he instructs her and Mordecai to write other letters in his name, and seal them with his seal, and send them to all the provinces in the empire, giving the Jews full liberty to defend themselves; which is accordingly done; and the letters are sent off with the utmost speed to all the provinces: in consequence, the Jews prepare for their own defense, <reference osisRef="Est.8.8-Est.8.14">Est 8:8-14</reference>. Mordecai appears publicly in the dress of his high office, <reference osisRef="Est.8.15">Est 8:15</reference>. The Jews rejoice in every place; and many of the people become Jews, because the fear of the Jews had fallen upon them, <reference osisRef="Est.8.16">Est 8:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Est.8.17">Est 8:17</reference>. <div eID="gen15593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15594" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen15594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15595" type="x-p"/> The king - give the house of Haman - As Haman was found guilty of treasonable practices against the peace and prosperity of the king and his empire, his life was forfeited and his goods confiscated. And as Mordecai had been the means of preserving the king's life, and was the principal object of Haman's malice, it was but just to confer his property upon him, as well as his dignity and office, as Mordecai was found deserving of the former, and fit to discharge the duties of the latter.
entries.dad11e0b4f57a948148eacc8aba9732e3b49005f: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen15595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15596" type="x-p"/> The king took off his ring - In the ring was the seal of the king. Giving the ring to Mordecai was tantamount to giving him the seal of the kingdom, and constituting him the same as lord chancellor among us.
entries.5a7c1992ce2339b282148a79c408399d4cab938d: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen15596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15597" type="x-p"/> To see the destruction of my kindred? - She had now informed the king that she was cousin to Mordecai, and consequently a Jewess; and though her own life and that of Mordecai were no longer in danger, Haman being dead, yet the decree that had gone forth was in full force against the Jews; and if not repealed, their destruction would be inevitable.
entries.9c1dfc17cbaff8c01001ef62cee3d200ea0abee5: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen15597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15598" type="x-p"/> May no man reverse - Whatever had passed the royal signet could never be revoked; no succeeding edict could destroy or repeal a preceding one: but one of a similar nature to the Jews against the Persians, as that to the Persians was against the Jews, might be enacted, and thus the Jews be enabled legitimately to defend themselves; and, consequently, placed on an equal footing with their enemies.
entries.61492fbde67d3e902f369f44b7afb7eaf916a3a7: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen15598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15599" type="x-p"/> The month Sivan - This answers to a part of our May and June.
entries.a233304aa9d2849607af1300eefe0c763c8dc232: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen15599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15600" type="x-p"/> On mules, camels, and young dromedaries - What these beasts were is difficult to say. The word רכש rechesh, which we translate mules, signifies a swift chariot horse. <div eID="gen15600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15601" type="x-p"/> The strange word אחשתרנים achashteranim is probably a Persian word, but perhaps incurably corrupted. The most likely derivation is that of Bochart, from the Persian akhash, huge, large, rough, and aster, a mule; large mules. <div eID="gen15601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15602" type="x-p"/> The words בני הרמכים beney harammachim, the sons of mares, which we translate dromedaries, are supposed to signify mules, produced between the he ass and the mare, to distinguish them from those produced between the stallion and the ass, But there is really so much confusion about these matters, and so little consent among learned men as to the signification of these words, and even the true knowledge of them is of such little importance, that we may well rest contented with such names as our modern translations have given us. They were, no doubt, the swiftest and hardiest beasts that the city or country could produce.
entries.ce2e917ef5edea729111a4d3d01cbf4e138fd0fc: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen15602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15603" type="x-p"/> To destroy, to slay, and to cause to perish - The same words as in Haman's decree: therefore the Jews had as much authority to slay their enemies, as their enemies had to slay them. <div eID="gen15603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15604" type="x-p"/> Little ones and women - This was the ordinary custom, to destroy the whole family of those convicted of great crimes; and whether this was right or wrong, it was the custom of the people, and according to the laws. Besides, as this edict was to give the Jews the same power against their enemies as they had by the former decree against them, and the women and children were there included; consequently they must be included here.
entries.eacaf531183e5066af8986f8afbda25b88547dc9: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen15604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15605" type="x-p"/> The decree was given at Shushan - The contrary effect which it was to produce considered, this decree was in every respect like the former. See <reference osisRef="Est.3.8-Est.3.15">Est 3:8-15</reference>.
entries.5386145d41b141ccd4a8486fd31c09f5880960f6: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen15605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15606" type="x-p"/> Blue and white - Probably stripe interchanged with stripe; or blue faced and bordered with white fur. <div eID="gen15606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15607" type="x-p"/> A great crown of gold - A large turban, ornamented with gold, jewels, etc. <div eID="gen15607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15608" type="x-p"/> Fine linen and purple - See on <reference osisRef="Gen.41.42">Gen 41:42</reference> (note). The בץ buts, here mentioned, is most probably the same with the byssus of the ancients; supposed to be the beautiful tuft or beard, growing out of the side of the pinna longa, a very large species of muscle, found on the coasts of the Mediterranean Sea, of which there are a pair of gloves in the British Museum. This byssus I have described elsewhere. <div eID="gen15608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15609" type="x-p"/> Shushan - was glad - Haman was too proud to be popular; few lamented his fall.
entries.7ef5b8eb8b9fb01776fec6a6f16c7a0d42bf5d99: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen15609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15610" type="x-p"/> Many - became Jews; for - fear - These were a species of converts not likely to bring much honor to true religion: but the sacred historian states the simple fact. They did profess Judaism for fear of the Jews, whether they continued steady in that faith or not. <div eID="gen15610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15611" type="x-p"/> It is only the Gospel which will not admit of coercion for the propagation and establishment of its doctrines. It is a spiritual system, and can be propagated only by spiritual influence. As it proclaims holiness of heart and life, which nothing but the Spirit of God can produce, so it is the Spirit of God alone that can persuade the understanding and change the heart. If the kingdom of Christ were of this world, then would his servants fight. But it is not from hence.  <chapter eID="Esth.8"/> <div eID="gen15611" type="x-p"/>

entries.04fcf4b9df474ccb5b9d38391f140ca71d2be4f2: <reference osisRef="Esth.8.1">Est 8:1</reference> <div eID="gen6784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6785" type="x-p"/> By the execution of Haman, his property was confiscated, and the king decreed that the house of the Jews’ enemy should be given to Esther. The “house of Haman” undoubtedly means the house with all that pertained to it. “And Mordochai came before the king, for Esther had told him what he was to her,” viz., her kinsman and foster-father, Est 2:7. This information effected Mordochai’s appearance before the king, i.e., his reception into the number of the high dignitaries who beheld the face of the king, i.e., were allowed personal access to him; comp. <reference osisRef="Esth.1.10">Est 1:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Esth.1.14">Est 1:14</reference>; Est 7:9.
entries.506541c8b717706f1952156829b72cfd255fd7f7: <reference osisRef="Esth.8.2">Est 8:2</reference> <div eID="gen6785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6786" type="x-p"/> And the king took off his seal-ring which he had taken from Haman (comp. <reference osisRef="Esth.3.10">Est 3:10</reference>), and gave it to Mordochai. מן העביר, to cause to go from some one, i.e., to take away. By this act Mordochai was advanced to the post of first minister of the king; comp. <reference osisRef="Gen.41.42">Gen 41:42</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.41.1">1</reference> Macc. 6:15. The king’s seal gave the force of law to royal edicts, the seal taking the place of the signature. See rem. on <reference osisRef="Esth.8.8">Est 8:8</reference> and Est 3:10.
entries.50cf916063aef3d0938a3f938143280e0dcb0882: <reference osisRef="Esth.8.3-Esth.8.4">Est 8:3-4</reference> <div eID="gen6786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6787" type="x-p"/> The chief enemy of the Jews was now destroyed; but the edict, written in the king’s name, sealed with the royal seal, and published in all the provinces of the kingdom, for the destruction of all the Jews on the 13th day of the twelfth month, was still in force, and having been issued in due legal form, could not, according to the laws of the Persians and Medes, be revoked. Queen Esther therefore entreated the king to annul the designs of Haman against the Jews. <reference osisRef="Esth.8.3">Est 8:3</reference> and Est 8:4. “Esther spake again before the king, and fell down at his feet, and wept, and besought him to do away with (העביר, to cause to depart) the mischief of Haman the Agagite, and his device that he devised against the Jews. And the king held out his golden sceptre towards Esther, and Esther arose and stood before the king.” This verse gives a summary of the contents of Esther’s speech, which is reported verbally in <reference osisRef="Esth.8.5">Est 8:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Esth.8.6">Est 8:6</reference>, so that we must translate the imperfects ותּתחנּן ותּבך - ותּפּל: She spoke before the king, falling at his feet and beseeching him with weeping, that he would do away with המן רעת, the evil that Haman had done, and his device against the Jews. The king stretched out his sceptre (comp. <reference osisRef="Esth.4.11">Est 4:11</reference>) as a sign that he would graciously grant her petition; whereupon she arose, stood before the king, and made known her request.
entries.7cac3a2d98b738c0856af66cc73065bda66a9fcb: <reference osisRef="Esth.8.5-Esth.8.6">Est 8:5-6</reference> <div eID="gen6787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6788" type="x-p"/> The introductory formula are in part similar to those used <reference osisRef="Esth.1.19">Est 1:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.5.4">Est 5:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Esth.5.8">Est 5:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.7.3">Est 7:3</reference>; but the petition referring to a great and important matter, they are strengthened by two new phrases: “If the thing is advisable (כּשׁר, proper, convenient, advantageous, a later word occurring again only <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.6">Ecc 11:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.10.10">Ecc 10:10</reference>, - in <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.21">Ecc 2:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.4-Eccl.4.5">Ecc 4:4-5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.10">Ecc 4:10</reference> of the same book, כּשׁרון) before the king, and if I be pleasing in his eyes, let it be written (let a writing be used, like <reference osisRef="Esth.3.9">Est 3:9</reference>), to frustrate (להשׁיב, i.e., to put out of force) the letters, the device of Haman ... which he wrote to destroy the Jews, who are in all the provinces of the king.” המן מחשׁבת, the device, the proposal of Haman, is added to הסּפרים, briefly to characterize the contents of the letters. On the matter itself, comp. Est 3:8. and Est 3:12. “For how shall I endure to see the destruction of my people?” The verbs וראיתי אוּכל are so combined that the second is governed by the first, וראיתי standing instead of the infinitive; comp. Ew. §285, <hi type="italic">c</hi>. ראה cons. בּ denotes an interested beholding, whether painful or joyous, of something; comp. Gen 44:34. מולרת in parallelism with אם denotes those who are of like descent, the family, members of a tribe.
entries.67e9018ce9265dd5b60f9116fc1673b4e771565a: <reference osisRef="Esth.8.7-Esth.8.8">Est 8:7-8</reference> <div eID="gen6788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6789" type="x-p"/> The king could not simply revoke the edict issued by Haman in due legal form, but, ready to perform the request of the queen, he first assures her of his good intentions, reminding her and Mordochai that he has given the house of Haman to Esther and hanged Haman, because he laid hand on the Jews (תּלוּ אתו, him they have executed); and then grants them permission, as he had formerly done to Haman, to send letters to the Jews in the king’s name, and sealed with the king’s seal, and to write בּעיניכם כּטּוב, “as seems good to you,” i.e., to give in writing such orders as might in Esther’s and Mordochai’s judgment render the edict of Haman harmless. “For,” he adds, “what is written in the king’s name and sealed with his seal cannot be reversed.” This confirmatory clause is added by the king with reference to the law in general, not as speaking of himself objectively as “the king.” להשׁיב אין refers to Esther’s request: להשׁיב יכּתב (<reference osisRef="Esth.8.5">Est 8:5</reference>). ונחתּום, <hi type="italic">infin. abs.</hi> used instead of the <hi type="italic">perfect</hi>.
entries.beb648cdff8ad03da9e7028eb80b4c99bc6207e5: <reference osisRef="Esth.8.9-Esth.8.14">Est 8:9-14</reference> <div eID="gen6789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6790" type="x-p"/> These letters were prepared in the same manner as those of Haman (<reference osisRef="Esth.3.12-Esth.3.15">Est 3:12-15</reference>), on the 23rd day of the third month, the month Sivan, and sent into all the provinces. “And it was written according to all that Mordochai commanded.” They were sent to the Jews and to the satraps, etc., of the whole wide realm from India to Ethiopia (see <reference osisRef="Esth.1.1">Est 1:1</reference>), while those of Haman had been issued only to the satraps, etc. The rest coincides with Est 3:12. ויּכתּב, and he (Mordochai) wrote. To show the speed with which the letters were despatched, (messengers) “on horseback, on coursers, government coursers, the sons of the stud,” is added to הרצים בּיד. רכשׁ is a collective, meaning swift horses, coursers; comp. 1Ki 5:8. אחשׁתּרנים (<reference osisRef="Esth.8.11">Est 8:11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Esth.8.14">Est 8:14</reference>) answers to the Old-Persian <hi type="italic">kschatrana</hi>, from <hi type="italic">kschatra</hi>, government, king, and means government, royal, or court studs. So Haug in Ewald’s <hi type="italic">bibl. Jahrb.</hi> v. p. 154. The older explanation, mules, on the other hand, is founded on the modern Persian estar, which, to judge from the Sanscrit <hi type="italic">açvatara</hi>, must in ancient Persian have been <hi type="italic">açpatara</hi>. רמּכים, ἁπ. λεγ. from רמּך, answering to the Syriac <hi type="italic">remakaa'</hi>, herd, especially a herd of horses, and to the Arabic <hi type="italic">ramaka</hi>, stud, is explained by Bertheau as a superlative form for the animal who excels the rest of the herd of stud in activity, perhaps the breeding stallion, while others understand it of the stud in general. The contents of the edict follow in <reference osisRef="Esth.8.11">Est 8:11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Esth.8.12">Est 8:12</reference> : “that the king allows the Jews in every city to assemble and to stand for their life (i.e., to fight for their lives, comp. <reference osisRef="Dan.12.1">Dan 12:1</reference>), to destroy, to slay, and to cause to perish all the power (חיל, military power) of the people and province that should assault them, children and women, and to plunder their property, upon a certain day,” etc. The appointed time is thus stated as in Est 3:13. The Jews were thus authorized to attack and destroy all enemies who should assault them on the day appointed for their extermination. <reference osisRef="Esth.8.13">Est 8:13</reference> coincides with <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Esth.3.14">Est 3:14</reference></hi>, with this difference, that the Jews are to be ready on this day to avenge themselves on their enemies. <reference osisRef="Esth.8.14">Est 8:14</reference> also is similar to <reference osisRef="Esth.3.15">Est 3:15</reference>, except that the expression is strengthened by an addition to הרצים as in <reference osisRef="Esth.8.10">Est 8:10</reference>, and by that of דּחוּפים, urged on, to מבהלים, hastened, to point out the utmost despatch possible. <div eID="gen6790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6791" type="x-p"/> The joy experienced throughout the kingdom at these measures.
entries.df2afc8ec2200d107b3e881ea3c4d8def547ef9d: <reference osisRef="Esth.8.15">Est 8:15</reference> <div eID="gen6791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6792" type="x-p"/> After transacting with the king this measure so favourable to the Jews, Mordochai went out from the king in a garment of deep blue and white material (comp. <reference osisRef="Esth.1.6">Est 1:6</reference>), and with a great crown of gold, and a mantle of byssus and purple. תּכריך, ἁπ. λεγ., in the Aramaean תּכריכא, a wide mantle or covering. The meaning is not, as Bertheau remarks, that he left the king in the garment which had been, according to Est 6:8., presented to him, nor that he left him with fresh tokens of his favour, clothed in a garment, crown, and mantle just bestowed on him, but that he left him in a magnificent state garment, and otherwise festally apparelled, that he might thus show, even by his external appearance, the happiness of his heart. Of these remarks, the first and last are quite correct; the second, however, can by no means be so, because it affords no answer to the question how Mordochai had obtained crown and mantle during his stay with the king and in the royal palace. The garments in which Mordochai left the king are evidently the state garments of the first minister, which Mordochai received at his installation to his office, and, as such, no fresh token of royal favour, but only his actual induction in his new dignity, and a sign of this induction to all who saw him issue from the palace so adorned. “The city of Susa rejoiced and was glad,” i.e., rejoiced for gladness. The city, i.e., its inhabitants on the whole.
entries.809df3edb384178dcea098740df88b5ba7fb54c7: <reference osisRef="Esth.8.16">Est 8:16</reference> <div eID="gen6792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6793" type="x-p"/> The Jews (i.e., in Susa, for those out of the city are not spoken of till <reference osisRef="Esth.8.17">Est 8:17</reference>) had light and gladness, and delight and honour.” אורה (this form occurs only here and <reference osisRef="Ps.109.12">Psa 109:12</reference>), light, is a figurative expression for prosperity. יקר, honour - in the joy manifested by the inhabitants of Susa at the prevention of the threatened destruction.
entries.a82368382c949aaa2986f6bf08ff4a1881aa12b0: <reference osisRef="Esth.8.17">Est 8:17</reference> <div eID="gen6793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6794" type="x-p"/> And in every province and city ... there was joy and a glad day, a feast day, comp. <reference osisRef="Esth.9.19">Est 9:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Esth.9.22">Est 9:22</reference>, while Haman’s edict had caused grief and lamentation, Est 4:3. “And many of the people of the land (i.e., of the heathen inhabitants of the Persian empire) became Jews, for the fear of the Jews fell upon them.” מתיהדים, to confess oneself a Jew, to become a Jew, a denominative formed from יהוּדי, occurs only here. On the confirmatory clause, comp. <reference osisRef="Exod.15.16">Exo 15:16</reference>; Deu 11:25. This conversion of many of the heathen to Judaism must not be explained only, as by Clericus and Grotius, of a change of religion on the part of the heathen, <hi type="italic">ut sibi hoc modo securitatem et reginae favorem pararent, metuentes potentiam Mardechaei.</hi> This may have been the inducement with some of the inhabitants of Susa. But the majority certainly acted from more honourable motives, viz., a conviction, forced upon them by the unexpected turn of affairs in favour of the Jews, of the truth of the Jewish religion; and the power of that faith and trust in God manifested by the Jews, and so evidently justified by the fall of Haman and the promotion of Mordochai, contrasted with the vanity and misery of polytheism, to which even the heathen themselves were not blind. When we consider that the same motives in subsequent times, when the Jews as a nation were in a state of deepest humiliation, attracted the more earnest-minded of the heathen to the Jewish religion, and induced them to become proselytes, the fact here related will not appear surprising. The Jews Avenged of Their Enemies. The Feast of Purim Instituted - Esther 9 <div eID="gen6794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6795" type="x-p"/> On the day appointed by both edicts, the Jews assembled in the towns and provinces of the kingdom to slay all who sought their hurt, and being supported by the royal officials, inflicted a great defeat upon their enemies (<reference osisRef="Esth.9.1-Esth.9.10">Est 9:1-10</reference>). At the queen’s desire, the king granted permission to the Jews in Susa to fight against their enemies on the following day also (<reference osisRef="Esth.9.11-Esth.9.15">Est 9:11-15</reference>), while in the other towns and districts of the kingdom they fought for their lives only on the 13th of Adar; so that in these places they rested on the 14th, but in Susa not till the 15th, and consequently kept in the latter the one day, in the former the other, as a day of feasting and rejoicing (<reference osisRef="Esth.9.16-Esth.9.19">Est 9:16-19</reference>). The observance of this day of resting as a festival, under the name of Purim, by all the Jews in the Persian monarchy, was then instituted by Esther and Mordochai (<reference osisRef="Esth.9.20-Esth.9.32">Est 9:20-32</reference>).  <chapter eID="Esth.8"/> <div eID="gen6795" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:p n="1">1 ON that day did the king Ahasuerus give the house of Haman <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">With all his Goods and Estate, which being justly forfeited to the King, he no less justly bestows it upon the Queen to compen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sate the danger to which <ns0:hi>Haman</ns0:hi> had exposed her.</ns0:note>, the Jews enemy, unto Esther the queen, and Mordecai came before the king <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">

                  <ns0:p n="7">7 Then the king Ahasuerus said unto Esther the queen, and unto Mordecai the Jew, Behold I have gi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven Esther the house of Haman, and him they have hanged <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">You see how ready I have been to grant your requests, and I do not repent of my Favour to you, and am ready to grant your further Desires, as far as the Law will permit me to do.</ns0:note> upon the gallows, because he laid his hand upon the Jews.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="9">9 Then were the kings scribes called at that time in the third month (that <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the month Sivan) on the three and twentieth <ns0:hi>day</ns0:hi> thereof <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Which was above two months after the former decree.
